title: What Is a Good Business Credit Score for a Loan?
summary: A good business credit score for a loan is usually 76+ on Experian Intelliscore Plus, 80+ on D&B PAYDEX, and 211+ on FICO SBSS. This guide shows lenders how to set score thresholds by model, product, and lender type, including SBA changes in 2026.
body_markdown:
A good business credit score for a loan is usually 76 or higher on Experian Intelliscore Plus and 80 or higher on D&B PAYDEX. On the 0–300 FICO SBSS scale, lenders treat 211 or higher as low risk. Because there is no universal "good" score, the right threshold depends on the scoring model, the loan product, and the lender's risk appetite.


According to[Chase](https://www.chase.com/business/knowledge-center/start/business-credit-scores) , score ranges vary by bureau and model, so a 75 on one scale can mean something different on another. That makes threshold-setting a real operational question for credit teams and a common source of confusion for borrowers.


This guide covers the risk tiers for each major model, typical personal credit minimums, and current SBA expectations. It closes with a practical framework for setting score cutoffs your team and borrowers can understand.


‍


### What Counts as a Good Business Credit Score by Model


Each bureau builds its score on a different scale with different risk bands. Lenders that compare scores across models need a shared tier map before they can set consistent approval rules.


#### Know the Risk Tiers for Each Major Model


The table below uses risk tiers published by[SoFi](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/credit-score-for-business-loan) . Across the 1–100 scales, a score around 76 or higher is commonly cited as good.


Scoring model Range Low risk Moderate or higher risk


Experian Intelliscore Plus 1–100 76–100 51–75 low-medium, 26–50 moderate, 11–25 moderate-high


Equifax Payment Index 0–100 80–100 Below 80


D&B PAYDEX 1–100 80–100 50–79 moderate


FICO SBSS 0–300 211–300 160–210 moderate


Chase notes that Intelliscore draws on both business and personal data, and that SBSS may include the owners' personal credit. That blend matters when a lender wants to separate business risk from owner risk in its decision logic.


#### Recognize the Other Business Scores Lenders Pull


Some lenders and bureaus also report scores built for specific risks, such as delinquency or business failure. Chase lists these ranges:


Score Range Notes


D&B SBFE Score 706–999 840 or higher signals low risk


D&B Delinquency Predictor 101–670 Predicts likelihood of late payment


Equifax Credit Risk Score 101–992 Predicts serious delinquency risk


Equifax Business Failure Score 1000–1880 Predicts likelihood of business failure


Because these scales do not overlap, a credit policy should always name the model next to the cutoff. A rule that says "minimum score 80" is incomplete until it specifies PAYDEX, Equifax Payment Index, or another model.


#### Understand What Moves a Business Credit Score


Chase identifies five main factors that shape business credit scores. Knowing them helps lenders read a score in context and helps borrower-facing platforms explain why a score changed.


- **Length of credit history:** Older, established credit files typically score better than thin or new files.
- **Payment history:** On-time payments to vendors and creditors carry the most visible weight.
- **Credit utilization:** Using a smaller share of available credit signals lower risk.
- **Public records:** Bankruptcies, liens, and judgments pull scores down.
- **Company size and industry risk:** Larger firms and lower-risk industries tend to score higher.


#### Factor in Personal Credit Minimums by Lender Type


Most small business lenders still review the owner's personal credit, especially for younger companies. SoFi reports that typical business loan minimums fall between 500 and 700, depending on the lender.


Lender type Typical personal credit minimum


Traditional banks About 680, often 700 or higher


Online and alternative lenders 600 or less


Equipment financing About 630, sometimes the low 500s because the equipment is collateral


SBA lenders without SBSS Typically 620–680 personal FICO, with 720 or higher giving the best chance


These bands show why one "good score" answer rarely fits every product. A 640 personal score may be workable for equipment financing yet fall short at a traditional bank.


#### Track SBA Credit Expectations in 2026


SBA screening changed this year. Under an[SBA procedural notice](https://www.sba.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/Procedural%20Notice%20-%20Sunset%20of%20SBSS%20Score%20-%20Supplemental%20Guidance%20Corrected%202.24.pdf) , lenders are no longer required to use FICO SBSS to screen 7(a) small loans of $350,000 or less as of March 2026.


Instead, lenders must evaluate creditworthiness the same way they would for similar non-SBA loans, considering business credit alongside the owner's personal score. SoFi notes that the historical SBSS prescreen minimum for 7(a) small loans was 155, which now works as a reference point only.


[NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/business/loans/learn/sba-loan-credit-score) , in a June 2026 update, reports that the SBA sets no official personal credit minimum. Lenders typically look for these personal scores:


SBA program Typical personal credit target Lender examples


SBA 7(a) 650 or higher Live Oak Bank at 650, First Federal Bank at 700


SBA 504 680 or higher Varies by lender


SBA Microloans 620 or higher Ascendus as low as 575


#### See How Score Tiers Shape Loan Terms


Credit scores rarely decide a loan alone. Lenders also weigh revenue, time in business, cash flow, and collateral when they set approval and pricing.


Stronger scores usually earn better rates, higher amounts, and longer terms. Weaker scores often lead to smaller amounts, higher rates, shorter terms, or a decline. That is why tier-based pricing matters as much as a single cutoff.

### Steps to Set Business Credit Score Thresholds for Loans


A clear framework turns scattered score ranges into rules your underwriters, partners, and borrowers can follow. These six steps work for direct lenders and embedded-finance platforms alike.


#### 1. Map Each Product to Its Primary Models


Start by listing which scores each product will use, since SBA 7(a), equipment, and line-of-credit programs may each rely on different data. Write the model name next to every cutoff so no rule is ambiguous across scales.


#### 2. Anchor Cutoffs to Published Risk Tiers


Use bureau risk bands as your starting point, such as 76 or higher on Intelliscore Plus or 80 or higher on PAYDEX. Adjust from there based on your own portfolio performance and loss tolerance.


#### 3. Set Personal Credit Floors by Lender Type


Match personal credit floors to your product and collateral position, using the lender-type bands from SoFi as a benchmark. A collateralized equipment product can usually support a lower floor than an unsecured term loan.


#### 4. Build Tiers Instead of a Single Pass or Fail Line


Define approval tiers that link score bands to amount, rate, and term, so a moderate-risk applicant can still receive a smaller or shorter offer. This approach keeps viable deals in the pipeline instead of declining them outright.


#### 5. Layer in Cash Flow, Revenue, and Time in Business


Pair score thresholds with revenue, time in business, cash flow, and collateral checks, since lenders weigh all of them together. Banking data can confirm cash flow when a thin business credit file makes the score less reliable.


#### 6. Route Declines Through a Waterfall


When an applicant misses your cutoff, send the file to a second-look lender or an alternative product rather than ending the journey. A decline waterfall helps borrower-facing platforms keep the customer while matching them to a better-fit offer.


‍


### Best Practices for Using and Improving Business Credit Scores


Thresholds work best when lenders apply them consistently and borrowers understand how to improve. These practices help both sides avoid the most common mistakes.


#### Explain Scores in Plain Language for Borrowers


Borrower-facing platforms should show which model a lender used and what tier the score falls into. A simple message such as "PAYDEX 72, moderate risk" gives a business owner more to act on than an unexplained decline.


#### Coach Borrowers on Building Business Credit


Businesses with thin files can strengthen their scores through a few proven habits. Sharing this guidance helps platforms grow future approval rates.


- **Open trade accounts:** Work with vendors that report payments to the business credit bureaus.
- **Pay on time:** Consistent on-time payments build the strongest payment history.
- **Keep utilization low:** Use a small share of available credit lines.
- **Dispute report errors:** Review business credit reports and correct inaccurate entries.
- **Space out applications:** Avoid submitting many credit applications at the same time.


#### Avoid Common Threshold Pitfalls


The most frequent mistake is setting a cutoff without naming the model, which creates errors when files arrive with different scores. Another is relying on a single score while ignoring cash flow, which can decline healthy young businesses with limited credit history.


Lenders should also revisit SBA screening rules after the March 2026 SBSS change. Policies that still require a 155 SBSS minimum for 7(a) small loans now reflect a historical standard rather than a current requirement.


#### Review Thresholds Against Portfolio Results


Score cutoffs should evolve as repayment data comes in after launch. Regular reviews show whether a tier is too strict and losing good deals, or too loose and adding avoidable risk.


‍


### Conclusion


A good business credit score for a loan is 76 or higher on Experian Intelliscore Plus and 80 or higher on D&B PAYDEX or the Equifax Payment Index. On FICO SBSS, the low-risk band starts at 211. Personal credit still carries weight, with typical floors ranging between the low 500s and 700 depending on lender type and collateral.


Lenders should name the model behind every cutoff, build tiered offers instead of hard declines, and pair scores with cash flow data. For borrower-facing platforms, clear explanations of score tiers help business owners understand decisions and improve their chances next time.


‍


### Frequently Asked Questions


#### Can You Get a Business Loan With a 600 Credit Score?


Yes, many online and alternative lenders accept personal credit scores of 600 or less, according to SoFi. Equipment financing may also work because the equipment acts as collateral, though borrowers should expect smaller amounts, higher rates, or shorter terms.


#### Do Personal Credit Scores Matter for Business Loans?


Yes, most small business lenders review the owner's personal credit, especially for newer companies. Chase notes that Intelliscore uses both business and personal data, and SBSS may include the owners' personal credit.


#### What Credit Score Do You Need for an SBA Loan in 2026?


The SBA sets no official personal credit minimum, according to NerdWallet. Lenders typically look for 650 or higher for 7(a), 680 or higher for 504, and 620 or higher for microloans. As of March 2026, lenders no longer have to use FICO SBSS to screen 7(a) small loans of $350,000 or less.


#### Is 80 a Good PAYDEX Score?


Yes, a PAYDEX score of 80 falls in the low-risk band of 80–100, based on SoFi's published tiers. It signals that a business generally pays its vendors on time.


#### How Do Lenders Check Business Credit?


Lenders pull business credit reports and scores from bureaus such as Dun & Bradstreet, Experian, and Equifax, often alongside the owner's personal credit. Many also review banking data, revenue, and time in business to confirm the score reflects current performance.
